extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and documenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness), including the factual inquiries, acceptable rationales, and required factual/findings support for combining or modifying prior art. Targeted to examiners evaluating patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis — 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote and rely upon the statutory standard (AIA 35 U.S.C. 103). Note that patentability is not negated by the manner in which the invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the specific teachings of cited references and any relevant background art needed to evaluate differences with the claims. See MPEP 2141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — differences between prior art and claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit findings comparing claim limitations to prior-art disclosures. Differences should be described with respect to the claim limitations at issue. See MPEP 2141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make factual findings about the skilled artisan's knowledge, training, and capabilities as of the effective date, to frame expectations of predictability and routine experimentation. See MPEP 2141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — objective evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate any objective evidence relevant to obviousness (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and weigh secondary considerations; articulate how they impact the obviousness analysis. See MPEP 2141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make findings of fact then provide a rationale for combining/modifying prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Any 103 rejection must address findings of fact and then provide a rationale for combining or modifying the teachings of the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with factual findings (what each reference teaches, factual differences, level of skill, evidence) and then explain why one of the recognized rationales makes the claimed combination or modification obvious. See MPEP 2143.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit rationale requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each rejection must contain an explicit rationale clearly explaining why it would have been obvious to combine or modify the teachings of the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on conclusory labels such as 'would have been obvious' or 'common sense' without explaining the technical reasoning and how it applies to the facts. See MPEP 2143; KSR guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address each included claim explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim included in a rejection must be explicitly addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must explain why the limitations of each included claim would have been obvious. It is not necessary to rewrite the entire rejection for every claim, but each claim's limitations should be tied to the factual findings and rationale. See MPEP 2143.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation required for every rationale used
rubrics_metrics.description: For each rationale deployed in an obviousness rejection, examiners must explain why the person of ordinary skill would have found the proposed modification obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to every type of rationale relied upon (e.g., substitution, optimization, obvious-to-try). Conclusory statements without reasoned explanation are insufficient to establish a prima facie case. See MPEP 2141 (I),(III); 2143.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — combining prior art elements yielding predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is a recognized rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how each element performs its known function and why combining them yields the predictable overall result; tie the explanation to the references' teachings. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — simple substitution of known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results is a recognized rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the substituted element would be expected to work in place of the prior element and why a skilled artisan would have made the substitution with a reasonable expectation of success. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — using known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products is a recognized rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the technique is known in the art and how applying it to the claimed subject would have a predictable beneficial effect recognized by the skilled artisan. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — applying a known technique to a device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results is a recognized rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the device was 'ready for improvement' and why the technique would have been applied with a reasonable expectation of success. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — choosing from a finite number of predictable solutions (obvious-to-try)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success ('obvious to try') can support an obviousness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the solutions were finite and predictable and that a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success. Mere conjecture about 'obvious to try' is insufficient. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — applying work from one field to prompt predictable variations in another
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or another field where the variations are predictable to a skilled artisan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the design incentives or market forces and predictability that would motivate the adaptations. Show how the cross-field teaching would lead to the claimed modification. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR rationale — teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led a skilled artisan to modify or combine references is an acceptable rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR rejected overly formalistic TSM but recognized that a teaching/suggestion/motivation in the prior art is one permissible rationale; tie any TSM assertion to specific disclosures or reasoning in the references. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping/approaching/similar ranges, amounts, proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlapping, approaching, and similar ranges, amounts, and proportions in prior art can support an obviousness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claimed ranges overlap or are close to prior-art ranges, show why the claimed ranges would have been obvious (e.g., overlap, predictability). Explain overlaps/close proximity for each included claim and specifically address ranges in dependent claims as needed. See MPEP 2144.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization within prior-art conditions / routine experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization within prior-art conditions or through routine experimentation can be a rationale, but differences in parameters (e.g., concentration, temperature) generally do not support patentability unless the optimization is shown to be more than routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate why routine optimization would have led to the claimed parameter and why the skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success. Presence of a result-effective variable is one possible motivation; examiners must make findings of fact and present underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail. See MPEP 2144.05 (II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-recognized equivalence for same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If the art recognizes two compositions or processes as useful for the same purpose, combining or substituting them may be prima facie obvious, but there must be an explanation of the art’s recognition of that utility/equivalence as of the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the art recognized the equivalence before the effective filing date and why substituting or combining would have been expected to work. Functional equivalence alone is insufficient absent evidence the art recognized that equivalence. See MPEP 2144.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using legal precedent as a source of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A line of reasoning drawn from legal precedent may support an obviousness rejection if the examiner shows how that legal reasoning applies to the facts of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on case law alone; show concrete factual parallels. Common TC1600 examples include automating manual activities, changes in size/shape/sequence of adding ingredients, and purifying old products. See MPEP 2144.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relying on common knowledge in the art and official notice limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on common knowledge without providing a reference only if they give a clear and unmistakable line of technical reasoning; statements of technical fact without documentary evidence qualify as official notice and are appropriate only where facts are capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration as well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, cite documentary references rather than relying on official notice. When using official notice, explain why the fact is universally known and instantaneously demonstrable. See MPEP 2144.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on common knowledge as principal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is never appropriate to rely on common knowledge as the principal evidence upon which a rejection is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent articulated rationale and supporting facts, stating that a combination is 'common sense' or 'intuitive' is insufficient. Provide concrete reasoning and, where possible, documentary support. See MPEP 2144.03 (A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must present factual findings and sufficient underpinning reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are required to make findings of relevant facts and present the underpinning technical/legal reasoning in sufficient detail to support a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual findings include what each reference discloses, differences with the claims, the level of ordinary skill, and any objective evidence. The rationale must tie these facts to one or more acceptable lines of reasoning. See MPEP 2141, 2143.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary requirement — explain obviousness of claim as a whole and of each limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness rejections must explain why the invention as a whole would have been obvious and why the limitations of each claim included in the rejection would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, explicit rejections allow applicants, examiners, and reviewers to understand the basis for the rejection; regardless of the rationale used, explain how it applies to the particular facts of the application and to each claim limitation. See MPEP 2141, 2143.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical examples illustrate adequate vs. inadequate rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples (e.g., spray pressure in meat treatment; substitution of antibiotics; counterion selection; codon optimization) demonstrate what constitutes adequate factual findings and reasoning versus inadequate, conclusory rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use example patterns: simple combination, simple substitution, overlapping ranges, optimization within prior art, teaching-suggestion-motivation. Adequate rationales tie specific reference teachings to claim limitations and show reasonable expectation of success; inadequate rationales are conclusory and fail to explain why routine optimization or similarity would have led to the claimed invention.
